input: When students begin to study heat transfer, one of the most important dimensionless quantities they will encounter is the Nusselt number, and it plays a crucial role in helping us understand how effectively heat is transferred at a surface. In essence, the Nusselt number can be thought of as a comparison between two different ways in which heat can move at a surface: on the one hand, convection, which is the transfer of heat into a moving fluid, and on the other hand, conduction, which is the transfer of heat through a stagnant layer of fluid. More precisely, the Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface, and this seemingly simple ratio actually tells us a great deal about which process is dominating in any given situation. When the Nusselt number is close to 1, this means that the two mechanisms are roughly comparable in size, and heat is essentially being transferred in much the same way as it would be if the fluid were barely moving at all, with conduction doing most of the work; a Nusselt number of exactly 1 would correspond to transfer by conduction alone. However, when the Nusselt number takes on a large value, this indicates that convection has become much stronger than conduction, and the movement of the fluid is now enhancing the transfer of heat very significantly compared with the purely conductive baseline. Overall, by keeping this interpretation firmly in mind, students can use the Nusselt number not merely as a number to be calculated, but as a meaningful indicator of the underlying heat transfer behaviour in a wide range of different situations.
target: The Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. Convection is heat transfer from a surface into a moving fluid. Conduction is heat transfer from the same surface through a stagnant layer of that fluid. The conductive rate is the rate the surface would show with the fluid at rest, and it is the fixed side of the comparison; the convective rate is the rate with the fluid in motion. A value near 1 means the two rates are nearly equal. Convection then adds little to what conduction alone would give, and the surface transfers heat almost as it would into still fluid; a value of 1 is the limiting case of transfer by conduction alone. A large value means the convective rate stands far above the conductive rate. Movement of the fluid then sets the transfer, and the conductive part is small by comparison. Between the two readings, the meaning moves with the ratio itself: the further the value stands above unity, the larger the share of the transfer that convection carries, and the less the result depends on the stagnant-layer rate. The number is a ratio of two rates of the same kind, so it carries no unit. Second-year work meets the number wherever a surface meets a moving fluid, and the reading is always the same comparison, stated before any calculation: near unity, conduction sets the rate; large, convection sets it.
